_about: The shared pattern catalog. Inherited by every profile; never duplicated per
profile, because two copies of a catalog drift within about two edits.
A profile may `disable` entries, `adjust` their severity, or add entries of
its own — see profiles/technical/ for the pattern.
SEVERITY is how much weight one hit carries: 3 strong, 2 moderate, 1 weak
alone. CONFIDENCE is how much the source material and our own testing trust
the pattern: `high` means it rarely fires on good human writing, `medium`
means it fires sometimes, `contested` means it fires on legitimate prose
often enough that it should never be actioned without reading the hit.
Severity and confidence are separate axes on purpose. An intensifier tic is
low severity and contested; vague attribution is moderate severity and high
confidence. Collapsing them into one number is how a scanner starts telling
people their own writing is fake.
AUTHORING GOTCHA: `kind: lexical` patterns are wrapped in \b(?:...)\b
automatically, so an alternation ending in a bare prefix will not match its
own inflections — `navigate the complex` never matches `complexities`,
because \b finds no boundary mid-word. Spell out whole-word alternatives,
or use `kind: structural`, which is passed through with no wrapping.
TIER is the axis that matters most, and it is coarser than severity.
Tier A entries are ARTIFACTS — leaked citation markup, chatbot register,
unreplaced placeholders. They are near-zero false positive and dispositive
on a single occurrence, so they carry `always_flag` and bypass density
gating entirely. Everything else is STYLE, is meaningful only in aggregate,
and is density-gated. If you add an entry, be honest about which it is;
style dressed up as an artifact is how a scanner starts making accusations.
CALIBRATION TARGET: the source reports that an expert LLM user tagging ten
pages as AI-generated has probably made one false positive. About 10% is
the realistic ceiling for human experts. Any tool claiming better precision
than that on style alone is overclaiming, this one included.
ERA matters. The source list tracks vocabulary by generation, and the
generations turn over fast: the 2023-24 cohort (delve, tapestry, testament)
is largely trained out, while the mid-2025-onward cohort is participial —
emphasizing, highlighting, showcasing, enhance. An entry's `era` field
records which cohort it belongs to. Patterns expire; re-check the sources.
NO SINGLE PATTERN INDICATES AI AUTHORSHIP. These fire together or they are
noise. The source page is blunt about this and so is this catalog:
'Humans are notoriously bad at distinguishing human and LLM-generated
text.' It cites a 2025 preprint finding that even heavy LLM users judge
correctly about 90% of the time — one wrong call in ten. It also notes that
non-native English speakers are taught to avoid repeating words, which
produces the same surface features this catalog looks for.
So: signals for an author to weigh about their own draft. Never a verdict,
and never a test to run on someone else's writing.
The source page adds a warning that is easy to over-read, so read it
precisely. It says do not treat these signs as the defects to be fixed,
because sanding them off 'could just make detection harder' WITHOUT
MAKING THE WRITING BETTER. That is written for curators triaging
submissions to a shared encyclopedia, where the harm is a reviewer being
evaded. It is not an argument against drafting with a model, and it is
not an argument against a rewriter existing.
The part that generalises is the second clause. A tell list is a symptom
list, and prose optimised to minimise it is bland rather than human —
which is why nothing downstream may use this catalog as a target. Give a
reviser the author's voice and corpus as its objective; give it this
catalog as one diagnostic among several.

wp-signs.title: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing
wp-signs.note: Canonical community-maintained list; least commercially motivated source available. Fetched and extracted directly for this catalog.

wp-talk.title: Wikipedia talk:Signs of AI writing (+ Archive 1, Archive 2)
wp-talk.note: Retrieved with both archives. This is what the `confidence` field is built on: it records which patterns editors treat as strong and which they argue about. It is also where `transition-overload` is recorded as tested and demoted — see the `rejected` block. Not read: Archive 3+, whose existence was not verified.

wp-cleanup.title: Wikipedia:WikiProject AI Cleanup
wp-cleanup.note: The remediation posture: verify before removing, check cited sources for legitimacy, preserve salvageable sources rather than deleting wholesale. Matters most for the revise pass in the prose-review bundle. Notably attaches no quantified confidence threshold to any of its tags.

recent.title: Secondary coverage of current-generation tells, 2025-2026
recent.note: Surveyed. Weight varies sharply and is recorded per entry. The strongest item is a 2026 arXiv study finding that purely STRUCTURAL narrative features separate AI from human fiction at 93.2% macro-F1 with no lexical features at all — which is the empirical case for this scanner's cadence half. The em-dash figures come from an independent 2026 measurement. Several widely repeated patterns trace to a single Forbes contributor piece with no dataset, and are labelled contested here. Much of the rest of this space is SEO marketing for detection and humanizer tools, with invented thresholds; none of it is used.

fixture.title: Observed in this repo's own regression fixture
fixture.note: script-v1-before.txt vs script-v2-after.txt — same author, same content, known answer.

local.title: Added during authoring, not yet corroborated by a primary source
local.note: Treat as provisional. Anything here should either earn a source or be dropped.

_about: Patterns deliberately NOT shipped, and why. Recorded rather than deleted
because a silently removed pattern gets re-added by the next person with
the same plausible idea. Everything here looked reasonable and lost.

transition-overload.was: Density of furthermore / moreover / additionally / it is worth noting.
transition-overload.why_rejected: Wikipedia's editors shipped this, tested it, and DEMOTED it to their Ineffective indicators section, on the reasoning that conjunction overuse 'is more of a byproduct of essaylike-writing that AI and humans engage in'. Their current page states only a few transition words are known to be overused. This catalog shipped it briefly in v0.1 and it immediately produced a false positive on this repo's own docs/wiring.md. Re-adding it repeats an experiment already run and already reverted.
transition-overload.replaced_by: didactic-disclaimer, which targets the narrower 'it is important to note' habit rather than conjunction density.

perfect-grammar.was: Flawless spelling and grammar as evidence of generation.
perfect-grammar.why_rejected: Listed as an ineffective indicator: many editors are skilled writers or come from professional writing backgrounds.

formal-register.was: Formal, academic, or elevated prose as evidence.
formal-register.why_rejected: Stated directly by the source: the correlation with AI 'does not extend to all formal, academic, or fancy-sounding prose'. This is also the failure mode that hits non-native English speakers hardest, and is the single most important thing this catalog must not do.

bland-or-robotic-prose.was: Prose that reads as flat or mechanical.
bland-or-robotic-prose.why_rejected: Listed as ineffective; usually reflects the reader's unfamiliarity with real AI patterns rather than a property of the text.

em-dash-density.was: Em dashes per 1000 words as a flagging signal.
em-dash-density.why_rejected: The numbers do not support it. A 2026 measurement REPORTEDLY puts the human baseline at mean 3.23 per 1000 words with a range of 0.33 to 17.12 — a fiftyfold spread — while current models have moved BELOW that mean (GPT-5.4 at 1.43, Gemini 2.5 Flash at 1.28). Only the aging 4.x generation sits clearly above it. CAVEAT, and it matters because these figures are the whole argument for this rejection: they come from `sources.recent`, the one source entry with no URL, so they are secondhand and currently uncitable — see the callout in the bundle README. The rejection does NOT rest on them alone. Wikipedia's talk page is independently its most-argued item, with editors calling it weak and noting the essay itself is full of them; and this repo's own docs measure 11-18 per 1000 first-hand, which a gate keyed on em dashes would flag. Em-dash rate is still MEASURED and REPORTED here, because it is useful context about a document's texture, but it never flags.

curly-quotes.was: Typographic quotes and apostrophes as evidence.
curly-quotes.why_rejected: Word processors have auto-formatted these for over a decade, and Gemini and Claude typically do not emit them at all. Measured and reported, never flagged.

synonym-expansion.was: Expanding flagged vocabulary into synonym sets.
synonym-expansion.why_rejected: The source is explicit: 'This section is to be taken as literally as possible: a word being overused by AI does not imply that its synonyms are also overused.' Entries here match the attested word, not its neighbourhood.

_about: Patterns the brief asks for that a regex genuinely cannot decide. Recorded
here so the gap is documented rather than quietly dropped, and so the
Phase 2 critics know what they own exclusively. Do not add regexes for
these — an approximation would fire on everything and teach people to
ignore the whole tool.
not_deterministic.llm-safe-truths: Unfalsifiable filler sentences that pad without adding information. Detecting them requires knowing what the sentence claims and whether the claim could be wrong.
not_deterministic.announced-then-undelivered: An insight announced and never actually delivered. Needs the surrounding argument.
not_deterministic.surveying-without-committing: Presenting positions without defending one. A whole-document property.
not_deterministic.absence-of-concrete-detail: No name, number, date, place, or quoted phrase where one belongs. Absence is not matchable.
not_deterministic.no-voice-shift: Register that never moves with subject matter. Requires comparison across sections.
not_deterministic.invented-specifics: Concrete-sounding detail that is fabricated. Requires checking against the world.

entries.label: model markup artifact
entries.note: Literal strings no human types: citation scaffolding from ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, and Perplexity that survived a copy-paste. These are ARTIFACTS, not style — dispositive rather than suggestive — so they bypass density gating entirely via always_flag. One occurrence is the finding.

entries.label: chatbot register leaked into the draft
entries.note: Assistant-to-user conversational register surviving into a document that has no user to address. Leakage, not style, so it barely false-positives.

entries.label: knowledge-cutoff or source-gap hedge
entries.note: A model describing its own epistemic position, or narrating the gaps in its retrieval. Neither belongs in a finished document.

entries.label: unreplaced placeholder
entries.note: Template text the author never filled in. Trivially checkable and embarrassing to ship, which makes it worth catching even though it is rare.

entries.label: delve
entries.note: The signature tell of the 2023-24 generation. Largely trained out, so a hit now is notable.

entries.label: tapestry (figurative)
entries.note: Figurative use only. Literal weaving is not matched.

entries.label: bustling
entries.note: Almost always promotional travel-brochure register.

entries.label: "in today's ... world" / "in an era of"
entries.note: The canonical throat-clearing opener.

entries.label: intricate
entries.note: Legitimate about genuinely intricate mechanisms; filler about ideas.

entries.label: underscore (figurative)
entries.note: Verb form with an abstract object only. The typography character and identifier naming are not matched, and `technical` allowlists it anyway.

entries.label: "navigate the complexities"
entries.note: Deliberately requires an abstract object. Navigating a menu, a tree, or a ship is not a tell. Note the whole-word alternatives: lexical entries are wrapped in \b automatically, so a bare prefix like `complex` would fail to match `complexities`.

entries.label: "ever-evolving landscape"
entries.note: Requires the modifier. Literal landscapes and 'the landscape of X' in geography are not matched.

entries.label: "foster a sense of"
entries.note: Requires the abstract object. Foster care and fostering animals are not matched.

entries.label: "dive into" / "deep dive"
entries.note: The replacement 'delve' was trained into. Same move, newer word.

entries.label: comprehensive
entries.note: A checkable factual claim in technical writing, filler everywhere else. Allowlisted in `technical`.

entries.label: robust
entries.note: Precise in statistics and systems engineering, filler in marketing. The clearest argument for per-register allowlists; allowlisted in `technical`.

entries.label: leverage (verb)
entries.note: Verb use with an object only, so financial and physical leverage are not matched. Allowlisted in `technical`.

entries.label: paradigm
entries.note: A term of art in programming and philosophy of science. Allowlisted in `technical`.

entries.label: genuinely
entries.note: Fine once. Six times in four thousand words is a tic, which is why this category is judged on density and never on presence.

entries.label: actually
entries.note: Top hit in the session that motivated this primitive: eight occurrences the model's own self-assessment did not notice. Counting is what scripts are for.

entries.label: quiet / quietly
entries.note: Named in recent coverage as a current-generation adverbial tic.

entries.label: crucially / importantly / interestingly
entries.note: Sentence-adverb throat-clearing. Legitimate sparingly.

entries.label: negative parallelism ("it's not X, it's Y")
entries.note: Widely treated as the strongest structural tell of the current generation, and reported at roughly 3x human rate — but the measurement behind that figure traces to a single news article, with no published corpus study. Confidence is `medium` rather than `high` for that reason, and because the source page itself concedes the construction is 'common among human writers'. FALSE POSITIVES ARE DOCUMENTED AND SERIOUS: autistic writers and anyone with a formal rhetorical education report using deliberate parallel construction for decades, and binary contrast is a structural resource of English itself. THE RULE THAT SURVIVES SCRUTINY IS FREQUENCY AND PURPOSELESSNESS, NOT PRESENCE — one deliberate contrast is rhetoric; five paragraphs ending on the same shape is autopilot. Which is why this is density-gated like everything else. Pivot may be a comma, semicolon, or em dash.

entries.label: "not just X, but Y"
entries.note: The compressed form of negative parallelism. Legitimate occasionally; a signature at volume.

entries.label: participle tail clause
entries.note: The tail that asserts significance instead of showing it. Restricted to significance-asserting verbs on purpose — generic tails (', allowing you to...') are ordinary English and would swamp this.

entries.label: announced insight
entries.note: Announcing that an insight is coming, in place of delivering one. PROVENANCE: not a named pattern in Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing; it traces to a Forbes contributor piece (Feb 2026) plus one independent observer, neither with counts or a control corpus. Downgraded from severity 3 accordingly. DIAGNOSTIC: if a plain 'But' carries the same content, the buildup was decorative. Also a genuine spoken-register idiom, so read the hit before cutting — narration especially. FP-2026-07-26-a: the 'best part' branch required no punctuation, so it matched the ordinary-English reading ('it was the best part of joining') while never actually requiring the announcing form. Now requires a following '?' or ':'. See CALIBRATION.md.

entries.label: false range ("from X to Y")
entries.note: A vague spectrum gestured at to imply comprehensiveness. TWO WARNINGS. (1) PROVENANCE: this is NOT in Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing — a targeted search of the raw wikitext found no such pattern. It was inherited from the design brief and is retained on this author's judgement alone, which is why severity is 2 and confidence is contested. (2) It over-fires: the prototype's version matched every date and number range ('From 1995 to 2003'). Numerals, currency, months, and weekdays are now excluded on both sides, and the construction must be sentence-initial or introduced by everything/ranging/spanning/covering.

entries.label: compulsive summary
entries.note: HISTORICAL. The source files this under indicators from roughly 2023 and treats it as obsolete in newer models — formulaic conclusion sections restating the body. A hit today points at an older draft or a human writing habit more than at a current model.

entries.label: "overall," / "in short,"
entries.note: Milder than the explicit summary markers and often legitimate. Separated so the strong form is not diluted by the weak one.

entries.label: didactic disclaimer ("it's important to note")
entries.note: Replaces the `transition-overload` entry, which was REMOVED — see the `rejected` block. This narrower form is the disclaimer habit, not conjunction density. Historical: the source dates it Nov 2022-2024 and calls it obsolete in newer models, so a hit is more likely an older draft than a current one.

entries.label: enumeration scaffolding
entries.note: Announcing the shape of a list before giving it. 'Three reasons, and each one is worth sitting with.'

entries.label: "whether you're X or Y"
entries.note: Direct-address audience enumeration; marketing-copy scaffolding.

entries.label: rule of three (X, Y, and Z)
entries.note: KNOWN NOISY, kept deliberately and gated hard on density. The tricolon is ordinary English — a single hit means nothing. What is informative is the RATE: models reach for three-item lists far more evenly than people do. Read this row as a measurement, never as a list of defects.

entries.label: stacked hedging
entries.note: Two hedges doing one hedge's work.

entries.label: significance assertion
entries.note: Asserting that something mattered instead of showing that it did.

entries.label: vague attribution
entries.note: High confidence because it is checkable: either the citation is there or it is not. The prose-substance-critic in the prose-review bundle inherits every hit.

entries.label: vibrant / rich / compelling
entries.note: Ordinary adjectives that cluster in generated prose. Weak alone, informative as a rate.

entries.label: current-era participles (emphasizing / highlighting / showcasing)
entries.note: The mid-2025-onward cohort, and the reason this catalog is not just a list of words from 2023. Where the older tells were nouns (delve, tapestry), the surviving ones are participles. Bare use is ordinary English, so this is density-gated and weak; the high-severity signal is the same verbs in a significance-asserting tail clause, which `participle-tail` catches separately.

entries.label: enhance / align with
entries.note: Also mid-2025-onward. Ordinary in technical writing; watch the rate, not the presence.

entries.label: "boasts a"
entries.note: Press-release verb. A building does not boast.

entries.label: "nestled in" / "in the heart of"
entries.note: Travel-brochure register, and one of the most distinctive single tells on the source list.

entries.label: "commitment to excellence"
entries.note: Press-release phrasing; the source list flags it via quoted executive statements.

entries.label: "stands as" / "serves as"
entries.note: Narrowed to the significance-asserting objects. 'Serves as the entry point' is ordinary technical prose and is not matched.

entries.label: "reflects a broader" / "part of a broader"
entries.note: Zooming out to significance the piece has not earned.

entries.label: the challenges-and-future-prospects formula
entries.note: A whole-paragraph shape the source list names explicitly: 'Despite its [positive descriptor], [subject] faces challenges...' closing on speculation about future improvement. Distinctive because it is a template, not a phrase.
